title: Two Rivals, Secret Rockets
summary: After the war, America and the Soviet Union each grabbed German rockets and built their own. Fruit flies, monkeys and brave little dogs rode rockets before any person did. In secret, a Soviet engineer who had once been a prisoner built the most powerful rocket in the world.

sections.heading: Treasure Hunters in the Ruins
paragraphs: In the summer of 1945, Germany lay in ruins. Cities were piles of broken brick, millions of people had lost their homes, and the country was split into four zones, each run by one of the winning powers: the United States, the Soviet Union, Britain and France. Moving through this wreckage were special teams of scientists and intelligence officers with lists of names and addresses. They were not looking for gold. They were looking for knowledge: jet engines, chemicals, radar and, above all, rockets.

The American effort began under the code name Operation Overcast and was soon renamed Operation Paperclip. The story usually told is that officials marked the files of the Germans they wanted with a paperclip. Its aims were simple: to use German know-how to help American weapons and science, and to stop that same know-how from going to the Soviet Union. Over the following years, about 1,600 German scientists, engineers and technicians, many with their families, were brought to the United States under Paperclip and related programmes.

The most famous group was the rocket team. Wernher von Braun, who had surrendered to American soldiers in May 1945, helped choose who should come. By February 1946, 118 German rocket specialists had arrived at Fort Bliss, an army base near El Paso, Texas, and the group soon grew to about 127. At first their life was strange and restricted. They lived in old wartime barracks in a fenced-off area, and they could only go shopping in El Paso with an American sergeant along. They played football, went bowling, watched films and learned to love Texas steaks. Their families started to arrive from Germany in December 1946.

This raised a hard question, and it is still debated today. Many of these men had worked for the Nazi regime. Some, like von Braun, had been members of the Nazi Party and the SS, and some had been involved in using forced labour at the Mittelwerk. President Harry Truman approved the programme but said that active Nazis should not be included. However, historians have shown that some officials in charge of the programme cleaned up or hid uncomfortable information in the scientists' records. Supporters argued that the United States could not afford to let the Soviet Union get all this expertise. Critics argued that people who may have shared responsibility for terrible crimes were given new careers and never faced justice. Both sides of that argument are part of the true history of spaceflight.

sections.heading: V-2s Over the Desert
paragraphs: Meanwhile, about 300 railway wagons full of V-2 parts, shipped across the Atlantic from the Mittelwerk, rolled into a remote stretch of New Mexico desert called White Sands. It was a perfect place for testing rockets: flat, dry, nearly empty of people, and surrounded by mountains. The US Army built a blockhouse with thick concrete walls and a launch area called Launch Complex 33. German and American engineers worked side by side, putting rockets together from the captured parts.

The first V-2 launched at White Sands, on 16 April 1946, lost one of its steering vanes and had to be shut down after 19 seconds. But soon the launches went better. Between 1946 and the early 1950s, about 67 V-2s were fired there. Instead of explosives, the nose carried scientific instruments. Scientists from universities and from the Naval Research Laboratory competed for space in the rocket's nose to measure cosmic rays, the Sun's ultraviolet light, temperatures and pressures high in the atmosphere, and how the air changes with height.

One of the most famous results came on 24 October 1946. A V-2 carried a 35-millimetre movie camera up to about 105 kilometres. The camera snapped a picture every second and a half. When the rocket fell back, the camera was smashed, but the film had been sealed inside a steel case and survived. When scientists developed it, they saw something no human had ever seen: grainy black-and-white pictures of Earth from space, with clouds, the curve of the horizon and the black sky above. Those were the first photographs ever taken from space.

Engineers also experimented with putting one rocket on top of another, the 'rocket train' idea that Tsiolkovsky had imagined decades earlier. In Project Bumper, a small American rocket called the WAC Corporal was mounted on the nose of a V-2. When the V-2 burned out, the smaller rocket lit and kept climbing. On 24 February 1949, the Bumper 5 flight reached about 400 kilometres high and a speed of more than 8,000 kilometres per hour, a record at the time. In July 1950, a Bumper became the first rocket ever launched from a new site in Florida called Cape Canaveral, which would later become one of the most famous launch sites in the world.

In 1950 the Army moved von Braun's team to Redstone Arsenal in Huntsville, Alabama. There they designed a new missile, the Redstone, which first flew in 1953. It was a direct descendant of the V-2, but American-built and more powerful. Von Braun also became a public figure, writing magazine articles and working with Walt Disney on television programmes in the 1950s that showed millions of Americans paintings and models of space stations and Moon ships. He talked about space; the Army mostly wanted missiles.

sections.heading: The Prisoner Who Became the Chief Designer
paragraphs: Now we cross to the other side of the world, and meet one of the most important people in the whole history of spaceflight, a man most of the world did not know existed until after he died.

Sergei Pavlovich Korolev was born in January 1907 in Zhytomyr, a city in what is now Ukraine. As a teenager he fell in love with flying, built gliders and studied engineering in Kyiv and then in Moscow. In the early 1930s he became one of the leaders of GIRD, the Moscow rocket club we met in part 6, and helped launch the GIRD-09 rocket in 1933. Then he worked at the Soviet Union's first official rocket institute, designing rocket-powered gliders and missiles.

In the late 1930s the Soviet dictator Joseph Stalin carried out the Great Purge, a time of terror when hundreds of thousands of people were arrested on false charges and many were executed. On 27 June 1938, Korolev was arrested, falsely accused of sabotage. He was sent to the Gulag, the network of Soviet prison labour camps, and spent months travelling by train and ship to the Kolyma region in the far north-east of Siberia, one of the coldest places on Earth. There he was forced to work in a gold mine. Prisoners there faced bitter cold, hunger and disease, and many did not survive. Korolev's health was badly damaged; he is said to have lost several teeth from scurvy, an illness caused by lack of vitamin C.

He was saved, in a strange way, by other prisoners. Stalin's government had set up special prison design offices, nicknamed 'sharashkas', where arrested engineers were made to keep working on aircraft and weapons. The famous aircraft designer Andrei Tupolev, himself a prisoner, asked for Korolev, and in 1940 Korolev was moved to Tupolev's prison workshop. Later he worked under another prisoner engineer, Valentin Glushko, on rocket engines to help aircraft take off. He was released in the summer of 1944, though he was only officially cleared of the false charges in 1957.

After the war, Korolev was sent to Germany as an officer to study the V-2. He was not interested in only copying it. He wanted to go much further. In 1946 he became head of a rocket department at a new research institute called NII-88 near Moscow, and in time he became the leader of his own design bureau, OKB-1. Inside the space programme everyone called him simply the 'Chief Designer'. Outside, his name was a state secret. When Soviet newspapers praised the great achievements of Soviet rockets, they never said who was behind them, and when Korolev wrote articles for the public, he used a false name, 'Professor K. Sergeyev'. His name was only revealed to the world in his obituary after he died in January 1966.

sections.heading: The Soviets Build Their Own V-2
paragraphs: The Americans had taken von Braun and most of the top German rocket leaders, along with the best parts. But the Soviet Union controlled Peenemünde, Nordhausen and the Mittelwerk tunnels, and many skilled German engineers and workers still lived nearby. In 1945 and 1946, Soviet engineers, including Korolev, Glushko and a young electrical engineer named Boris Chertok, set up institutes in central Germany. At first one was based in the town of Bleicherode, and later the work was gathered into larger organisations in the Nordhausen and Bleicherode area. There, Soviet and German engineers together rebuilt the V-2 from leftover parts, collected the scattered drawings and figured out how to make the rocket again.

Then, on the night of 22 October 1946, Soviet officials suddenly woke up more than 2,000 German specialists, many with their families, and put them on trains to the Soviet Union, whether they wanted to go or not. Many ended up on Gorodomlya, a small island in Lake Seliger, north-west of Moscow, where they worked under the leadership of a German engineer named Helmut Gröttrup. They proposed clever new rocket designs, but the Soviet leaders, and Korolev himself, increasingly preferred to rely on their own engineers. The Germans were gradually cut off from the important work, and by the early 1950s most were allowed to go home.

In October 1947, the Soviets launched their first rebuilt V-2s from Kapustin Yar, a new test site on the dry steppe near the Volga River. A year later came the R-1, a Soviet-made copy of the V-2 built from Soviet materials and factories. Test flights began in the autumn of 1948, and although many early rockets failed, the R-1 was soon working well enough to enter service with the Soviet army in 1950. It was not an exciting new design, but making it taught Soviet industry how to build every part of a large liquid-fuel rocket. Korolev quickly moved on to longer-range rockets, the R-2 and then the R-5, each going farther than the last.

So, by around 1950, both rivals had their own V-2 copies and teams busy improving them. In the United States, the German team was one of several groups, competing with the Army, Navy and Air Force and with companies. In the Soviet Union, Korolev's group was becoming the heart of the whole programme. Neither side knew everything the other was doing. That secrecy, and the fear that came with it, would shape the next twenty years.

sections.heading: Bombs, Oceans and the Cold War
paragraphs: To understand why both governments poured so much money into rockets, we have to talk about the most frightening weapon ever made. In August 1945, the United States dropped atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, helping to end World War II but killing well over 100,000 people. For four years, America was the only country with such bombs. Then, on 29 August 1949, the Soviet Union tested its own atomic bomb. In the early 1950s, both countries went on to build hydrogen bombs, which were hundreds of times more powerful still.

This was the start of the Cold War, a long rivalry between the United States and its allies on one side and the Soviet Union and its allies on the other. It was called 'cold' because the two superpowers never fought each other directly in a full war. Instead, they competed in almost everything: weapons, spying, sport, science and, before long, space. Each side was afraid that the other might attack first.

At first, the only way to deliver a nuclear bomb across the world was by a large bomber plane. Bombers were slow, taking many hours to fly between continents, and they could be spotted by radar and shot down. A rocket was different. A rocket big enough to throw a bomb thousands of kilometres would fly up through space and down onto its target in about half an hour, and nothing could stop it. Such a weapon is called an intercontinental ballistic missile, or ICBM. 'Ballistic' means that after its engines stop, it simply falls along a curved path, like a thrown ball. It needed a range of thousands of kilometres, at least ten times farther than the V-2 could fly.

For the Soviet Union, the ICBM mattered even more than for the United States. America had air bases in Europe and Asia close to the Soviet Union, so American bombers could reach Soviet cities fairly easily. Soviet bombers, however, would have had to fly all the way across the Arctic or the oceans to reach America. A rocket that could cross the world was the Soviets' way of catching up. That is why, in the early 1950s, the Soviet government gave Korolev the go-ahead to build a gigantic rocket. Early Soviet hydrogen bombs were also very heavy, so the missile had to lift a warhead of around 5 tonnes, which forced Korolev to design something far larger than anyone had built. That giant size would turn out to be very important for space.

sections.heading: Flies, Monkeys and Dogs Go First
paragraphs: Before any human could ride a rocket, scientists wanted to know: can a living creature survive the shaking of launch, the crushing push of acceleration, the weightlessness of free fall and the radiation high above the atmosphere? No one knew. So the first passengers were animals.

The very first animals sent into space and brought back alive were tiny fruit flies. On 20 February 1947, American scientists put them, along with some corn seeds, into a capsule called Blossom on the nose of a V-2 at White Sands. Fruit flies were chosen because scientists already knew a lot about their genes, so they could check whether radiation had harmed them. The rocket reached about 109 kilometres in just over three minutes. Then the Blossom capsule was thrown off, its parachute opened, and when it was found in the desert, the flies were still alive.

Next came monkeys. Several rhesus monkeys, all named Albert, rode V-2s from White Sands. On 14 June 1949, Albert II reached about 134 kilometres, making him the first monkey, and the first mammal, in space. Sadly, his parachute failed and he died when the capsule hit the ground. Several of the early animal flights ended like this, which is part of why these experiments still make many people uncomfortable today. Scientists of the time argued they were the only safe way to learn whether space was survivable before risking a human life.

The Soviet Union chose dogs. Soviet scientists picked small stray dogs from the streets of Moscow, believing that dogs who had survived cold winters and hunger would be tough and calm. They chose dogs that weighed about 6 to 7 kilograms so they would fit in small cabins, and mostly female dogs, partly because a special suit for collecting waste worked better for them. Light-coloured dogs were preferred because they showed up better on the cameras that filmed them. The dogs were trained for weeks: sitting quietly in small boxes, wearing their suits and getting used to loud noise and vibration.

In the summer of 1951, two dogs named Dezik and Tsygan, whose name means 'Gypsy', rode a modified R-1 rocket to an altitude of about 100 kilometres. Their cabin came back down by parachute, and both dogs were found alive and well. They were the first dogs to make a suborbital flight. Tsygan never flew again; a senior Soviet scientist, Anatoli Blagonravov, took her home as a pet. Dezik was less lucky and died on a later flight with another dog named Lisa when the parachute failed. Over the 1950s, dozens of dogs made rocket flights, many of them more than once. Their brave little journeys helped engineers design the cabins, parachutes and life-support systems that would later keep human cosmonauts alive.

sections.heading: The Semyorka: A Bundle of Five Rockets
paragraphs: Korolev's giant missile was called the R-7, and its engineers nicknamed it 'Semyorka', which means 'little seven' or 'number seven' in Russian. It was unlike anything built before.

The problem was simple to state and very hard to solve: no single rocket engine of the time was strong enough to lift such a heavy missile. Korolev's answer was to bundle rockets together. In the middle stood a long central core. Strapped around it were four tapered boosters, which made the rocket look a little like a bunch of carrots or a fat skirt at the bottom. The engines came from Valentin Glushko's design bureau. Each of the five parts had one engine with four combustion chambers and nozzles, so at liftoff the R-7 fired 20 main nozzles at once, plus smaller steering engines. It burned kerosene with liquid oxygen. Fully fuelled, it weighed about 280 tonnes, more than 20 times as much as a V-2, and it stood about 31 metres tall.

There was another clever trick. In the 1950s, nobody was sure that a large liquid-fuel engine could be safely started high up in the thin air after the rocket had already been flying. So Korolev's team lit all the engines, the core and all four boosters, on the ground at the same time. After about two minutes, the four empty boosters fell away and the core kept burning. This meant the R-7 was really a two-stage rocket, but with both stages running at liftoff. The rocket did not stand on its tail on the launch pad; it hung from strong metal arms over a huge pit, so the flames could pour down into a deep trench. As it rose, the arms swung back like the petals of an opening flower.

To launch it, the Soviets built a new secret base on the flat, empty steppe of Kazakhstan, near a railway stop called Tyuratam. Construction started in 1955, in a place of blazing summers, freezing winters and dust storms. Today this site is known as the Baikonur Cosmodrome, and it is still in use.

The first R-7 launch, on 15 May 1957, ended when a fire in one booster made the rocket break up. The next attempts also failed. Then, on 21 August 1957, an R-7 roared off its pad and flew about 6,000 kilometres across the Soviet Union, landing its dummy warhead in the target area on the Kamchatka Peninsula in the far east. The warhead broke apart as it came back into the thick air, a problem engineers would still need to fix. But the rocket itself had worked. It was the world's first successful flight of an ICBM. On 27 August, the Soviet news agency TASS announced to the world that the Soviet Union had a 'super-long-distance' multistage ballistic missile. Many people in the West were not sure whether to believe it. The American Atlas ICBM had not yet made a successful flight.

There is one more amazing fact about the R-7. Its basic design, a core with four strap-on boosters and engines all lit at liftoff, is still flying today as the Soyuz rocket, which has launched cosmonauts, astronauts and countless satellites. The R-7 family has flown more often than any other family of rockets in history. A rocket designed in the 1950s to carry a nuclear bomb ended up becoming one of humanity's most reliable spaceships.

sections.heading: A Year for Science, and a Race Nobody Announced
paragraphs: While the military raced in secret, scientists around the world were planning something peaceful. They called it the International Geophysical Year, or IGY, and it ran from 1 July 1957 to 31 December 1958, about 18 months. Scientists from 67 countries agreed to study the Earth together: the oceans, the weather, earthquakes, the poles, the Sun's effects on our atmosphere and the glowing northern and southern lights. Research stations were set up in Antarctica, and ships and balloons gathered data all over the world.

In 1954, the scientists organising the IGY suggested that countries should try to launch an artificial satellite during it, a small object circling the Earth to measure conditions in space. The United States took up the challenge. On 29 July 1955, the White House announced that America would launch 'small earth-circling satellites' as part of the IGY. President Dwight Eisenhower and his advisers also had a quieter reason. They wanted to establish the principle of 'freedom of space', the idea that a satellite flying over another country was not breaking into its airspace. This would make it legal, later, to use spy satellites to watch the Soviet Union.

Only a few days later, in early August 1955, at a scientific meeting in Copenhagen, the Soviet scientist Leonid Sedov announced that the Soviet Union would launch a satellite too. Few people in the West paid much attention.

The Americans now had to decide whose rocket to use. Von Braun's team offered a plan called Project Orbiter, using a Redstone missile with small extra rocket stages on top. Instead, a committee chose a new rocket called Vanguard, designed by the Naval Research Laboratory. Part of the reason was that Vanguard was a scientific rocket, not a military missile, so it fitted the peaceful image the United States wanted, and it would not disturb the Army's missile work. Project Vanguard officially began in September 1955. Its planned satellite was tiny, about the size of a grapefruit and weighing less than 2 kilograms in its first version.

But Vanguard was a brand-new rocket that had to be designed from scratch, and that took time. Meanwhile, von Braun's team in Huntsville was testing a souped-up Redstone called the Jupiter-C. On 20 September 1956 it flew more than 1,000 kilometres high. Its top stage was not a real rocket, but a dummy filled with inert material, and many people have wondered since whether the team could have reached orbit if they had been allowed to try. Historians still argue about it.

By the autumn of 1957, the IGY had begun, Vanguard was still not ready, and the Soviets had a working giant rocket that had just flown across Siberia. Korolev, who had been dreaming of space since his GIRD days, had persuaded his government to let him use an R-7 to launch a simple satellite. In the CIA and the Pentagon, some officials suspected something might happen soon. But most Americans had no idea. Then, on the night of 4 October 1957, radio operators around the world picked up a strange new signal from the sky: beep... beep... beep. It was coming from space, and the whole world was about to be surprised.

deepDive: Historians often describe the period from 1945 to 1957 as one in which captured German technology gave both superpowers a head start, but in very different ways. The United States got most of the senior German engineers, including von Braun, and about 100 rockets' worth of parts. Yet for years the American rocket effort was split among the Army, Navy and Air Force, each with its own projects, and missiles had low priority until the early 1950s, partly because long-range bombers already seemed good enough. The Soviet Union got fewer top Germans but put its own engineers, led by Korolev, Glushko and others, firmly in charge, and used the Germans mostly as a source of knowledge before sending them home. Soviet leaders, lacking bases near America, also had a stronger reason to fund ICBMs early. A key technical turning point came with the hydrogen bomb. In 1954, an American committee led by the mathematician John von Neumann concluded that thermonuclear warheads would soon be light and powerful enough that an ICBM could carry one and did not need to hit its target precisely. This made the Atlas missile a top national priority. The Soviets, whose early warheads were heavier, built the R-7 to carry about 5 tonnes, which is why it was so large, and why it could later lift satellites and crewed spacecraft. Its first stage and boosters together produced roughly 400 tonnes of thrust at liftoff. The R-7's flight on 21 August 1957 is usually called the first successful ICBM test, although its warhead disintegrated on re-entry; heat shields for warheads took further work in both countries. Another debate is moral. Operation Paperclip brought scientists into the United States despite official rules against admitting active Nazis, and historians and writers such as Michael Neufeld and Annie Jacobsen have shown how records were sometimes softened. Supporters stress the Cold War context; critics point to the forced labourers who died at the Mittelwerk. Animal flights raise their own ethical questions. Today, researchers still debate how much the space race was driven by science and how much by weapons; in this period the honest answer is that rockets were built mainly as weapons, with science and exploration riding along, sometimes literally, in their nose cones.
funFact: The first photographs of Earth taken from space were shot on 24 October 1946 by a movie camera riding a captured V-2 from New Mexico; the camera was smashed on landing, but the film survived inside a steel case.
